prompt: 1.5.0 is crashing on 1011 phones. Under what condition can a minimum version of 1.5.1 reach them?

choices.text: If Google Play is asked to push the update to them
choices.why: No store pushes a version into a phone.

choices.text: If the person opens the store
choices.why: Then they could update anyway; the screen is the app's.

choices.text: If 1.5.0 already reads the minimum at start-up
choices.why: Right. The check ships before the version it refuses.

choices.text: Never; installed versions cannot be reached
choices.why: They can, through code they already contain.

prompt: Match each installed version to what the planner does, with minimum 1.5.1 and latest 1.6.0.

pairs.right: a screen that cannot be dismissed
a prompt that can be dismissed

prompt: What does iOS offer an app that wants to force an update, compared with Android's In-App Updates?

choices.text: No API: the app checks and links to the store
choices.why: Right. The minimum comes from your server.

choices.text: A setting in App Store Connect that blocks old versions
choices.why: No such setting exists.

choices.text: Silent updates the app can trigger
choices.why: Apps cannot update themselves.

choices.text: The same immediate and flexible flows
choices.why: Those are Google Play's.

prompt: Google Play's update priority ranges from 0 to what number?
Put the planner's sources of configuration in the order it tries them.
On a first launch with no network and no cache, the planner 1.5.0 was allowed to run. Why is that right?

choices.text: 1.5.0 was fine all along and never needed the minimum
choices.why: It was below the minimum; the defaults did not know.

choices.text: The server allowed it
choices.why: The server was down.

choices.text: The cache was corrupted
choices.why: There was no cache.

choices.text: Safe defaults never lock people out on an outage
choices.why: Right. That is the price, and the right one.

prompt: Which of these does not belong in remote configuration? Choose every one.

choices.text: An API secret
choices.why: Right. Anything downloaded can be read.

choices.text: Whether this person has paid
choices.why: Right. Access is decided on the server.

choices.text: The share of installs that see a new screen
choices.why: That is what flags are for.

choices.text: The minimum supported version
choices.why: That belongs there.

prompt: A configuration value sets the sync timeout. Somebody sets it to 0 by mistake. What should the app do?

choices.text: Use 0, since the server is the source of truth
choices.why: The app validates what it receives.

choices.text: Reject it and use its default
choices.why: Right. Every value is checked against a range.

choices.text: Crash, so the mistake is noticed
choices.why: A crash punishes the person for the team's mistake.

choices.text: Ask the person what to use
choices.why: Nobody can answer that.

prompt: Why does the bucket hash include the flag's name as well as the installation's id?

choices.text: To make the hash longer
choices.why: Length is not the point.

choices.text: So each flag reaches a different 20%
choices.why: Right. Not the same people for every new feature.

choices.text: So killed flags hash differently
choices.why: Killed flags are off before any hash.

choices.text: Because sha256 requires two inputs
choices.why: It takes any input.

prompt: In the lesson, for how many of 1000 installs was the statistics flag on?
A reviewer sees the planner without the statistics screen, because it is behind a flag at 0%. The review notes say nothing. What is wrong?

choices.text: Statistics screens need a permission
choices.why: No permission is involved.

choices.text: Nothing; flags are invisible to the stores and their reviewers
choices.why: Invisible is exactly the problem.

choices.text: The flag should be set to 100% and left there for good
choices.why: Rollout is fine; hiding from review is not.

choices.text: The flags turn on a feature the reviewer never saw
choices.why: Right. The build should show every feature its flags can enable, and the notes say how.

prompt: Match each kind of flag to how long it should live.

pairs.right: until 100%, then removed with the old path
until the test has its answer

prompt: How many combinations of on and off do ten independent flags make?

choices.why: Right. Two to the tenth.
Two per flag, multiplied, not added.
Each flag doubles, it does not add one.
That is ten squared.

prompt: The usual rule is a ticket to remove a release flag, created in the same pull ___ that adds it.
Which of the lesson's tools could have switched off 1.5.0's broken feature within minutes?

choices.text: A forced update to 1.5.1
choices.why: It works only after each person updates.

choices.text: A new minimum in App Store Connect
choices.why: No such setting exists.

choices.text: A flag around the feature, shipped in 1.5.0
choices.why: Right. The kill switch, read at the next launch.

choices.text: Halting the rollout
choices.why: That protects only the phones without it.

prompt: Why does the lesson warn against a forced update every month?

choices.text: It makes updating a chore
choices.why: Right. The opposite of the goal.

choices.text: It breaks the minimum version
choices.why: It uses it.

choices.text: Both stores limit the forced updates a month
choices.why: No such limit; the cost is the people's.

choices.text: It uses too much battery
choices.why: Battery is not the concern.
